description: Production versus productivity, how firms raise output per worker, and how economies of scale reduce average cost.
content_html:
Production vs Productivity: Not the Same Thing

Production refers to the total output a firm creates — for example, a car factory assembling 500 vehicles in a week. Productivity is different: it measures how much output is generated per unit of input, usually per worker. A factory that makes 500 cars using 50 workers has labour productivity of 10 cars per worker per week.

Why does the distinction matter? A firm can increase production simply by hiring more workers or buying more machinery — that is just doing more of the same. Increasing productivity means getting more output from the same inputs, which lowers the cost of producing each unit. That is what makes a firm genuinely more competitive.

Key Fact

Labour productivity = total output ÷ number of workers. Higher productivity means more output from the same workforce, so average cost per unit falls — giving the firm a competitive advantage.

How Firms Raise Productivity

Three main routes drive up productivity. First, investment in training: workers who understand their tasks better make fewer mistakes and work faster. A supermarket checkout operator who is trained to handle self-service machines can supervise four tills instead of one, quadrupling their personal output.

Second, investment in technology and capital equipment: replacing manual processes with machines raises output without increasing headcount. Amazon’s fulfilment warehouses use robotic picking systems that handle thousands of parcels per hour — far beyond what manual sorting could achieve. New machinery often embodies the latest technological advances, so every £1 invested buys more productive capacity than the previous generation of equipment.

Third, better organisation through specialisation: when workers focus on one task they become more skilled and faster at it. A GP surgery that employs one receptionist to handle all admin, one nurse to carry out routine checks, and one doctor to make clinical decisions is more productive than if each person tried to do everything. The division of labour (covered in the resource allocation unit) underpins this logic.

Imagine two rival bakeries. Bakery A employs 10 workers and bakes 200 loaves a day. Bakery B employs 10 workers and bakes 400 loaves a day. Production is higher at Bakery B — but what matters competitively is productivity: Bakery B produces 40 loaves per worker per day versus 20 at Bakery A. Bakery B’s average cost per loaf is roughly half that of Bakery A’s, assuming similar wages and materials. Bakery B can therefore charge a lower price and still make the same profit margin — or charge the same price and earn a higher profit. This is why governments and firms both try to raise productivity rather than simply expand production.

Economies of Scale

As a firm grows and increases its output, its average cost — the cost of producing each unit — often falls. This happens because fixed costs are spread across more units, and because large firms can operate more efficiently. The fall in average cost that comes from increasing the scale of production is called economies of scale.

To picture this without a graph: imagine a small bakery rents its premises for £1,000 a month and produces 1,000 loaves. Its rent cost per loaf is £1. If the same bakery expands and produces 10,000 loaves using the same premises, the rent cost per loaf falls to just 10p. The fixed cost has been “diluted” across a much larger output. Now add in the efficiency gains below, and average cost falls even further.

Key Fact

There are five main types of internal economy of scale: purchasing (bulk-buying discounts), technical (specialist machinery), managerial (dedicated expert managers), financial (lower borrowing costs), and risk-bearing (spreading risk across product lines). All reduce average cost as output rises.

The Five Types of Internal Economy of Scale

Purchasing economies: Large firms buy raw materials and components in bulk and negotiate lower prices per unit. A supermarket chain ordering ten million tins of baked beans pays a fraction of the price per tin that a corner shop pays. This lowers the variable cost per unit sold.

Technical economies: Large firms can afford specialist, high-capacity machinery that smaller firms cannot justify purchasing. A mass-market car manufacturer uses robotic welding lines that work continuously with high precision. The high fixed cost of the equipment is offset by the enormous volume produced — the cost per car is very low.

Managerial economies: A large firm can employ specialists — a marketing director, a finance director, an operations manager — who are experts in their field. A small firm cannot afford to hire all these people, so its owner must do everything, usually less efficiently. Each specialist improves output in their area, lowering average cost across the business.

Financial economies: Large, well-established firms are seen as lower-risk by banks and investors, so they can borrow money at lower interest rates. A small start-up might pay a higher interest rate on a business loan because lenders fear it might fail. The lower interest payments for a large firm reduce its costs and improve profitability.

Risk-bearing economies: Large firms often operate across several markets or product lines. If one product line performs poorly, the others can compensate. A small firm selling only one product has all its risk in one place. By spreading risk, the large firm faces less uncertainty, which can lower its cost of capital and encourage investment.

Diseconomies of scale occur when a firm grows so large that its average cost begins to rise instead of fall. The most common cause is poor communication and coordination in very large organisations. When a company employs thousands of people across multiple sites, messages get distorted, decisions take longer to make, and workers can feel disengaged — reducing motivation and productivity.

A small independent restaurant can adjust its menu overnight in response to customer feedback. A national restaurant chain must route the same change through regional managers, head office approval, and supply chain teams — a process that can take weeks. This management inefficiency pushes up costs per unit. It is one reason why some large firms choose to break their operations into smaller, semi-autonomous units rather than running everything centrally.

Economies of Scale and Competitiveness

When a firm benefits from economies of scale, its average cost falls below that of smaller rivals. This gives it two strategic options: it can charge a lower price and win market share, or it can charge a similar price to competitors and earn a higher profit margin. Either way, it has a competitive advantage. This is why large supermarkets, airlines, and car manufacturers can often undercut smaller rivals — their scale reduces the cost of each unit they produce or sell.

It also explains a key pattern in modern economies: industries where economies of scale are very large tend to be dominated by a small number of huge firms. Once a firm gains scale advantages, it becomes very hard for new, smaller entrants to compete on price. This creates barriers to entry and is one reason why some markets have only a few dominant players.
exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to Explain economies of scale, you must give a chain of reasoning, not just a list. For example: “If a supermarket buys goods in bulk, it gets a discount on unit cost → this lowers its average cost → which allows it to charge a lower price than rivals → so it gains a competitive advantage.” Two common mistakes: (1) confusing ‘production’ with ‘productivity’ — always define both if asked; (2) stating that ‘average cost falls as output rises’ without explaining why — you must name the specific economy of scale (purchasing, technical, etc.) and connect it to the cost reduction. For Evaluate questions on growth, remember that diseconomies of scale mean growth does not always lower average cost — this is your counter-argument.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Production is total output; productivity is output per worker. Higher productivity lowers average cost and is the real source of competitive advantage.
  • Economies of scale mean average cost falls as output rises, through purchasing, technical, managerial, financial and risk-bearing economies. Large firms gain a cost advantage over smaller rivals.
  • Diseconomies of scale can reverse this benefit if a firm grows too large — communication and coordination problems push average costs back up.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is the correct formula for labour productivity?
A) Total cost divided by number of workers
B) Total output divided by number of workers
C) Total revenue divided by total cost
D) Total output divided by total cost
practice_questions.marks: B) Total output divided by number of workers. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A firm produces 6,000 units per week and employs 40 workers. Calculate the firm's labour productivity. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the correct method: labour productivity = total output ÷ number of workers = 6,000 ÷ 40; 1 mark for the correct answer of 150 units per worker per week.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way a manufacturer could increase its labour productivity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a valid method (e.g. invest in worker training / invest in new machinery / introduce greater specialisation / adopt new technology); 1 mark for explaining how this increases output per worker; 1 mark for a further development, such as explaining the impact on average cost (e.g. average cost per unit falls, improving competitiveness or profit margin).

practice_questions.text: SunFresh is a small fruit juice company that produces 50,000 bottles a month. It is considering expanding its factory to produce 500,000 bottles a month. Explain how economies of scale could benefit SunFresh if it expands.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a relevant economy of scale (e.g. purchasing economies — buys fruit in bulk at lower price per unit; technical economies — can justify specialist bottling machinery; managerial economies — can employ a dedicated operations manager; financial economies — larger firm may borrow at lower interest rates); 1 mark for explaining the mechanism (e.g. bulk buying lowers the cost of raw materials per bottle); 1 mark for a second economy of scale with explanation; 1 mark for explaining the consequence for SunFresh (e.g. average cost per bottle falls, so SunFresh can charge a lower price than rivals and gain market share, or earn a higher profit margin).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how an increase in productivity at a large car manufacturer could improve its performance in the market.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A well-developed chain of reasoning that links higher productivity to lower average cost, and then to at least two market outcomes (e.g. lower prices to gain market share AND/OR higher profit margin), with a clear link to competitive advantage over rivals. The response identifies a specific mechanism for the productivity increase (e.g. investment in robotic assembly) and explains the effect clearly.

Secure (3–4 marks): A clear explanation of how higher productivity reduces average cost and improves at least one market outcome (e.g. lower price or higher profit). Some development but the chain may not be complete or may stop at average cost without connecting fully to market performance.

Developing (2 marks): Some relevant points made (e.g. productivity means more output, costs go down) but the chain of reasoning is limited and the impact on market performance is not clearly explained.

Emerging (1 mark): A basic, undeveloped point about productivity or cost with little or no connection to market performance.

practice_questions.text:
"The best way for a firm to reduce its average costs is to grow as large as possible."
Do you agree with this view? Justify your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
- Economies of scale mean that as output rises, average cost typically falls. Large firms benefit from purchasing economies (bulk-buying discounts), technical economies (specialist machinery spread over high output), managerial economies (expert staff), financial economies (lower borrowing rates) and risk-bearing economies.
- A very large firm can achieve significantly lower average costs than rivals, allowing it to undercut on price or earn higher profit margins — both clear competitive advantages.
- In industries with high fixed costs (e.g. car manufacturing, airlines), growth is essential to dilute those costs across enough output to be viable.

Arguments against:
- Diseconomies of scale: beyond a certain size, communication and coordination problems push average costs back up. A firm that is too large becomes harder to manage efficiently.
- Growth alone does not guarantee lower average costs — the firm must also raise productivity. If workers become demotivated in a large bureaucratic organisation, output per worker falls and average cost rises.
- Some firms can achieve low average costs through productivity improvements without becoming very large (e.g. investing in technology or training).
- The optimal scale varies by industry: in some sectors (e.g. specialist craft goods, local services), small firms have lower average costs because personalisation and quality are more important than volume.

Judgement: The statement is partially correct — growth does lower average costs up to a point, and economies of scale are a powerful source of cost advantage. However, the strength of this effect depends on the industry and on whether the firm manages growth well. For cost-sensitive, volume-driven industries, growth is the clearest path to lower average costs. For service-based or niche markets, productivity improvements may be more effective than scale alone. A supported conclusion that distinguishes between industries or recognises the diseconomies limit should be rewarded.

Mastering (8–9): Developed arguments on both sides with specific economies of scale named and explained; clear judgement with reasoned justification referencing the size of the effect, the industry type, or the risk of diseconomies.
Secure (6–7): Both sides addressed with some development; judgement present but may lack full support.
Developing (3–5): Some relevant points on one or both sides; limited or absent judgement.
Emerging (1–2): Basic points with little development; no judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of economy of scale occurs when a large firm can borrow money at a lower interest rate than a small firm?
The fall in average cost per unit that results from a firm increasing its total output is called _____ of scale.
Diseconomies of scale occur when a firm grows too large and average cost begins to _____ instead of fall.
Match each economy of scale to its description:
right: Buying raw materials in bulk to get a lower price per unit
Using specialist high-capacity machinery only viable at large output
Employing expert specialist managers in each business function

flashcard_questions.q: What is the formula for labour productivity?
flashcard_questions.a: Labour productivity = total output divided by number of workers.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between production and productivity?
flashcard_questions.a: Production is total output; productivity is output per worker.

flashcard_questions.q: A firm produces 800 units with 20 workers. What is its labour productivity?
Name three ways a firm can increase its labour productivity.
flashcard_questions.a: Investment in training, new technology/capital, and better specialisation.
The fall in average cost per unit that occurs as a firm increases its total output.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a purchasing economy of scale?
flashcard_questions.a: Buying in bulk to get a lower price per unit from suppliers.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a technical economy of scale?
flashcard_questions.a: Using specialist, high-capacity machinery that only large output volumes can justify.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a managerial economy of scale?
flashcard_questions.a: Employing specialist managers in each function, improving efficiency across the firm.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a financial economy of scale?
flashcard_questions.a: Large firms borrow at lower interest rates because banks see them as lower-risk.
The rise in average cost when a firm grows so large it becomes difficult to manage.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do diseconomies of scale occur?
flashcard_questions.a: Poor communication, slower decision-making, and lower worker motivation in very large firms.

flashcard_questions.q: How does a rise in labour productivity affect average cost?
flashcard_questions.a: Average cost per unit falls, because more output is produced from the same workforce.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does average cost fall as output rises (economies of scale)?
flashcard_questions.a: Two reasons: fixed costs are spread across more units (reducing fixed cost per unit), and efficiency gains such as bulk-buying discounts reduce variable cost per unit too.

glossary_terms.definition: The total amount of goods or services made by a firm over a given period.
A measure of how efficiently inputs are turned into output, typically expressed as output per worker.
The output produced per worker in a given time period, calculated as total output divided by number of workers.
The cost of producing one unit of output, calculated as total cost divided by total output.
The reduction in average cost per unit that occurs as a firm increases its total output.
The rise in average cost that occurs when a firm grows too large and becomes harder to manage efficiently.

Factors that make it difficult or expensive for new firms to enter a market and compete, including economies of scale advantages, patents, government licences, high start-up costs, brand loyalty, and vertical integration.
